title: Common Risk Factors in the Returns on Stocks and Bonds
research_question: Which systematic factors explain the cross-section of average returns on stocks and bonds, and do shared factors link the return variation in these two asset classes?
data_description: The study uses U.S. stock returns from NYSE, AMEX, and (later) NASDAQ firms covered by CRSP, combined with accounting data from Compustat to construct portfolios sorted on size (market equity) and book-to-market equity. The bond side draws on returns for U.S. government bonds across maturity buckets and corporate bonds across credit-rating categories. Returns are monthly. The sample spans roughly 1963 through 1991. Test assets include 25 size and book-to-market sorted stock portfolios and a set of government and corporate bond portfolios. Candidate explanatory variables include the excess return on the value-weighted market portfolio, a size-mimicking spread (small minus big), a value-mimicking spread (high minus low book-to-market), a term-structure spread (long-term government bond return minus short-term Treasury), and a default spread (long-term corporate minus long-term government bond return).
institutional_context: The paper is set against a backdrop of accumulating empirical evidence that average stock returns are not fully captured by market beta alone: firm size, leverage, earnings/price, and book-to-market equity each appear related to expected returns, while the bond literature emphasizes maturity and default risk as drivers of bond returns. Stocks and bonds had typically been studied in isolation, with separate risk factors for each market. The institutional setting is the broad U.S. capital market — common stocks listed on major exchanges and publicly traded U.S. government and corporate bonds — over a multi-decade period. This setting motivates examining whether a parsimonious set of shared risk dimensions, capturing equity-style characteristics together with bond-market term and default conditions, can jointly describe expected returns across both asset classes.
